items.note: Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra described: 83 chapters, about 7,000 verses, covering site testing, settlement types, roads, buildings, forts, temples, images, paintings, machines.
items.gloss: The huge Vastushastra or Samarangana-sutradhara is unique and detailed from the viewpoint of town planning; though of 83 chapters and some seven thousand verses it is said to be incomplete; it covers land testing, types of settlements, roads, drains, types of buildings, forts, temples, images, paintings, machines and much else.

items.note: Bhoja as builder: references show he built over a hundred prāsādas in Dhārā alone and laid it out systematically.
items.gloss: Raja Bhoja was himself a great builder; references make clear he built over a hundred palaces in his capital Dhara alone; he planned Dhara in an orderly way.

items.note: Bhoja built temples and schools in Malwa and Mewar, temples at the four boundaries and Mahākāla at Ujjain; his architectural expertise shown by Yuktikalpataru and Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra.
items.gloss: He built many temples and schools in Malwa and Mewar; to bind India together religiously he built Kedara, Rameshvara, Somanatha and Mundira temples on the boundaries and the Mahakala temple at central Ujjain; in this he was a master of vastushastra and its construction subtleties, as both Yuktikalpataru and Samarangana-sutradhara show.

items.note: Table of contents of the Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra, including prāsāda chapters: Meru etc. sixteen prāsādas, 64 prāsādas, Drāviḍa, Nāgara and Bhūmija prāsādas, maṇḍapas, jagatī, liṅga-pīṭha and pratimā.
items.gloss: The headings include: presence of Brahma and Vishvakarma, creation after dissolution, land testing, town settlement, vastu, drains, vastupurusha, royal residence, house types, gates, foundation rites, vastu worship, measures of pitha, yantra rules, characteristics of the sthapati, prasada characteristics, the sixteen prasadas beginning with Meru, 64 prasadas beginning with Rucaka, Dravida prasadas, Nagara prasadas, Bhumija prasadas, mandapas, 27 mandapas, jagati, linga-pitha and images, and more.

items.note: Continuation of the Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra headings: Drāviḍa, Nāgara, Bhūmija prāsādas, maṇḍapas, jagatī, liṅga-pīṭha, pratimā-lakṣaṇa, 64 hasta-lakṣaṇa.
items.gloss: ... Dravida prasada, Nagara prasada, Digbhadra and other prasadas, Bhumija prasada, mandapa, 27 mandapas, jagati and its parts, linga-pitha and images, bhumibandha, lepyakarma, image characteristics, hand gestures (64), etc.; the subtle details under these headings present the whole world of vastu.

items.note: Author's explanation of the title 'Samarāṅgaṇa-sūtradhāra' via the Malwi word 'raṇathal' for a roof.
items.gloss: In Malwa making a roof is called making ranathal; the traditional roof of brick and lime is beaten with thin wood; with the ranathal done, the vastu work is complete; ranathal is a corruption of ranasthal, and as samarangana is a synonym of ranasthal the name Samarangana-sutradhara becomes meaningful.

items.note: Bhoja kept poetic form even in dry grant-charters; the opening Śiva verses of his copper plates.
items.gloss: Even in the copper plates of dry administrative orders Raja Bhoja did not let the poetry suffer: 'Victory to Vyomakesha, who bears on his head the lunar line, shaped like the sprout of the seed of the world; may the matted locks of the foe of Smara, tawny like lightning rising at the end of the aeon, ever bring you welfare.'

items.note: Bhoja's verse pair opens Paramāra copper-plate grants from Saṃvat 1074 to 1256 - a chancery tradition of about two centuries.
items.gloss: This verse pair used by Bhoja is found at the start of Paramara copper plates of Malwa continuously from Samvat 1074 to 1256; the tradition begun by Bhoja continued for nearly two centuries.

items.note: Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra's three types of country - jāṅgala (dry), anūpa (watery), sādhāraṇa (middling) - with their features (water, soil, climate).
items.gloss: Countries are of three kinds: jangala, anupa and sadharana; jangala is a region where water is far, mostly saline, with small thorny bushes, dry, hot, windy, black soil; anupa is low, with abundant water, many fish, rivers, and oily, big trees; sadharana is neither too cold nor too hot, having features of both.

items.note: Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra: sites with fresh stable water, gardens, tanks and stepwells, easy for vehicles, are praised for a town.
items.gloss: Surrounded by durva grass, herbs, munja, kusha, with sweet clear still water; endowed with vastu, sacrifice and temples, full of gardens, adorned all round with tanks and stepwells; easy for vehicles, delightful to couples, bringing prosperity - such lands are praised for a town.

items.note: Lands with cool sweet water, free from raiders, are suitable for founding khetas, villages and towns.
items.gloss: Land between grass and sea-like expanses, whose water is cold and sweet, is good; land not fit for raids by wicked people, giving shelter to many, free of tumult and fear, pleasing to the mind - on such lands villages, hamlets and towns should be founded.
